meta.description: Every number in nn-internals. Do not hand-edit.

steps.label: dL/dŷ
steps.note: The very first gradient. Everything downstream is this number, reshaped and rescaled by the chain rule.

steps.label: dL/dz2
steps.note: Identity output activation. The gradient is unchanged.

steps.label: dL/dW2
steps.formula: z2 = W2·a1 + b2  ⟹  dL/dW2 = dL/dz2 ⊗ a1ᵀ
steps.note: THIS is why activations are stored. To know how much W2 is to blame, you must know what W2 was multiplied by -- and that was a1, computed during the forward pass and kept in memory ever since.

steps.label: dL/db2
steps.note: A bias adds itself in unchanged, so it receives the gradient unchanged.

steps.label: dL/da1
steps.note: The gradient crosses the layer boundary. Note it reads the WEIGHTS here, not the activations -- a linear layer's input-gradient depends on its weights, its weight-gradient depends on its input.

steps.label: dL/dz1
steps.note: Hidden unit 2 had z1 = -0.8, so ReLU clamped it to 0 and its gradient is now exactly 0. It contributed nothing to the prediction, so it takes none of the blame. A dead unit.

steps.label: dL/dW1
steps.formula: z1 = W1·x + b1  ⟹  dL/dW1 = dL/dz1 ⊗ xᵀ
steps.note: Same story as W2, one layer down: the weight gradient is the output gradient times the saved input. Row 2 is all zeros -- the dead ReLU unit propagated its zero backwards.

steps.label: dL/db1
steps.note: Biases again receive the gradient untouched.

recipes.name: bf16 Adam, fp32 master, bf16 grads
recipes.note: optimizer = fp32 master 4 + m 4 + v 4; the common '16 bytes per parameter' figure

recipes.name: bf16 Adam, fp32 master, fp32 grads
recipes.note: some frameworks accumulate gradients in fp32

recipes.name: bf16 8-bit Adam, fp32 master
recipes.note: optimizer = fp32 master 4 + m 1 + v 1 (quantised states)

per_tensor.name: loss
per_tensor.note: the scalar the whole backward pass hangs off

timeline.label: idle
timeline.desc: Between iterations. Only the model and the optimizer's memory of it are resident.

timeline.label: load batch
timeline.desc: The input arrives on the device.

timeline.label: forward: ReLU
timeline.desc: a1 = relu(z1). The mask is kept so backward knows which units were active.

timeline.label: loss
timeline.desc: Peak ACTIVATION memory. Every saved forward tensor is still live and nothing has been freed yet.

timeline.label: backward: dL/dW2, dL/db2
timeline.desc: Reads the saved a1 to form the weight gradient -- and that is a1's last read, so it is released here, not at teardown.

timeline.label: backward: dL/da1, dL/dz1
timeline.desc: Crosses the ReLU. Reads the mask, then releases it. dL/da1 is consumed by dL/dz1 in this same phase.

timeline.label: backward: dL/dW1, dL/db1
timeline.desc: Reads the saved input x. All parameter gradients now exist -- and this is the peak.

timeline.label: graph teardown
timeline.desc: backward() returns. The remaining forward tensors and the loss scalar that rooted the call go out of scope.

timeline.label: optimizer step
timeline.desc: Reads the parameter gradients and the Adam moments, updates the weights in place.

timeline.label: zero_grad
timeline.desc: Gradients released. set_to_none=True actually frees them; set_to_none=False only writes zeros and keeps the buffers.

timeline.label: idle
timeline.desc: Back to the floor. Weights and optimizer state persist into the next iteration; everything else was temporary.

bitviews.label: a tiny gradient
bitviews.why: fp16 FLUSHES THIS TO ZERO — bf16 keeps it. This is the underflow that loss scaling exists to prevent.

bitviews.label: a small gradient
bitviews.why: below fp16's smallest normal value, so fp16 stores it as a subnormal and loses most of its precision.

bitviews.label: a large activation
bitviews.why: beyond fp16's maximum finite value of 65504, so fp16 overflows to infinity. bf16 has fp32's exponent range and is unbothered.

reference_configs._source: published model architecture parameters; external to this model, quoted not derived
reference_configs.mfu_note: Real training reaches roughly 35-50% of the dense peak (model FLOPs utilisation). Anything above ~55% for a large transformer should be treated as suspicious. Use a stated MFU rather than peak.
